node.period_rationale: International roots in 1981–85 (Corrigan; Corrigan and Sayer) fall in period_2, but the Canadian field's selected milestones (Kinsman 1987, Valverde and Weir 1988, Valverde 1991, Strange 1995, Strange and Loo 1997) and its critiques (1994–97) fall in 'Further turns, c. 1985–2000'. Matches groups.json.
node.date_label: International roots (Corrigan 1981; Corrigan and Sayer 1985) · Kinsman 1987 · Valverde and Weir 1988 · Valverde 1991 · critiques 1994–97 · Strange and Loo 1997 · selected publication milestones, not boundaries; coverage through 2000

node.description: Studies how morality, sexuality, health and conduct were made objects of governance by reformers, churches, professions, courts and the state, and how regulation shaped the selves of the regulated. The concept came into historical sociology through Philip Corrigan's work (1981) and Corrigan and Sayer's The Great Arch (1985), which treated English state formation as a cultural revolution; Ruonavaara describes their framework as fusing Durkheimian and Foucauldian analysis with Marxist theory. In Canada, Mariana Valverde and Lorna Weir offered preliminary remarks on moral regulation in Resources for Feminist Research (1988), and Valverde's The Age of Light, Soap, and Water (1991) argued that Protestant social-purity reformers were not simply repressive and that they linked sexual health to racial purity and slum clearance. Kinsman's The Regulation of Desire (1987), and later The Canadian War on Queers (2010, with Gentile), examined sexual regulation and the national-security campaign against gays and lesbians. Studies of contraception and eugenics (McLaren), women, girls and the law (Backhouse, Lévesque, Dubinsky, Strange, Sangster), welfare and single mothers (Little), and postwar normality (Adams, Gleason) widened the field. Adams tied moral regulation to state formation through venereal-disease policy, and Strange and Loo surveyed law and moral regulation from 1867 to 1939 (1997). Critics reformulated the concept: Dean (1994) recast Corrigan's account through Foucault's governmentality, and Ruonavaara (1997) rejected a monolithic, state-only project. The liberal order framework (McKay 2000) is a separate entry, closer to a history of capitalism.
node.scope_note: A research field, international in its theory and Canadian in most of its historical work. The liberal order framework is a separate project, 'closer to history of capitalism' (user, 2026-10-12); state formation (Curtis) is shared ground, not membership. Feminist legal and sexual history overlaps cdn_women_gender; youth and normality overlaps cdn_childhood_youth. Roster inclusion does not mean a scholar adopts the moral-regulation framework.
node.representative_figures_and_works: International roots: Corrigan, "On Moral Regulation" (1981); Corrigan and Sayer, The Great Arch (1985). Canadian work: McLaren and McLaren, The Bedroom and the State (1986); Kinsman, The Regulation of Desire (1987); Valverde and Weir, "The Struggles of the Immoral" (1988); Lévesque, La norme et les déviantes (1989); McLaren, Our Own Master Race (1990); Valverde, The Age of Light, Soap, and Water (1991); Backhouse, Petticoats and Prejudice (1991); Mitchinson, The Nature of Their Bodies (1991); Dubinsky, Improper Advances (1993); Adams, "In Sickness and in Health" (1994) and The Trouble with Normal (1997); Little, "Manhunts and Bingo Blabs" (1994); Valverde, ed., Studies in Moral Regulation (1994); Strange, Toronto's Girl Problem (1995); Strange and Loo, Making Good (1997); Gleason, Normalizing the Ideal (1999). Critiques and reformulations: Dean (1994); Hunt (1997, 1999); Ruonavaara (1997); Valverde, Diseases of the Will (1998). Extension: Sangster, Regulating Girls and Women (2001); Kinsman and Gentile, The Canadian War on Queers (2010).

representative_people.name: Philip Corrigan
representative_people.context: Introduces moral regulation as a concept of historical sociology; an international root, not a Canadian founder.
representative_people.works: "On Moral Regulation" (1981); The Great Arch (1985, with Sayer)

representative_people.name: Derek Sayer
representative_people.context: Co-author of The Great Arch, which treats English state formation as cultural revolution.

representative_people.name: Mariana Valverde
representative_people.context: With Lorna Weir, offers preliminary remarks on moral regulation (1988); argues that Protestant social-purity reformers in English Canada were not simply repressive and linked sexual health to racial purity and slum clearance; edits Studies in Moral Regulation; later studies alcohol and the "diseases of the will".
representative_people.works: "The Struggles of the Immoral" (1988, with Lorna Weir); The Age of Light, Soap, and Water (1991); Studies in Moral Regulation (1994, ed.); Diseases of the Will (1998)

representative_people.name: Lorna Weir
representative_people.context: Sociologist (York University) and co-author with Valverde of preliminary remarks on moral regulation (1988); title-level only.
representative_people.works: "The Struggles of the Immoral" (1988, with Valverde)

representative_people.name: Gary Kinsman
representative_people.context: A sociologist's history of sexual regulation in Canada, and of the national-security campaign against gays and lesbians from the 1950s to the 1990s.
representative_people.works: The Regulation of Desire (1987); The Canadian War on Queers (2010, with Gentile)

representative_people.name: Patrizia Gentile
representative_people.context: Co-author of the history of national security as sexual regulation (post-2000).
representative_people.works: The Canadian War on Queers (2010, with Kinsman)

representative_people.context: Studies contraception and abortion (with Arlene Tigar McLaren) and eugenics in Canada.
representative_people.works: The Bedroom and the State (1986, with A. T. McLaren); Our Own Master Race (1990)

representative_people.name: Constance Backhouse
representative_people.context: A legal historian of women and law in nineteenth-century Canada; later of racism and law (see cdn_immigration_ethnicity).

representative_people.name: Andrée Lévesque
representative_people.context: Francophone study of norms and "deviant" women in interwar Quebec. Also in cdn_women_gender.

strands.title: State formation as cultural revolution
strands.focus: Corrigan and Sayer's historical sociology of English state formation and its Canadian uses, as in Adams on VD policy. Curtis's census history is shared ground with the liberal order framework, not membership.
strands.works: Philip Corrigan, "On Moral Regulation: Some Preliminary Remarks," Sociological Review 29, no. 2 (1981): 313–337.; Philip Corrigan and Derek Sayer, The Great Arch: English State Formation as Cultural Revolution (Oxford: Basil Blackwell, 1985).; Mary Louise Adams, "In Sickness and in Health: State Formation, Moral Regulation, and Early VD Initiatives in Ontario," Journal of Canadian Studies 28, no. 4 (1994): 117–130.; Bruce Curtis, The Politics of Population: State Formation, Statistics, and the Census of Canada, 1840–1875 (Toronto: University of Toronto Press, 2001).

strands.title: Moral reform and social purity
strands.focus: Protestant reformers, social purity and law; reform as a productive, not only repressive, project.
strands.works: Mariana Valverde and Lorna Weir, "The Struggles of the Immoral: Preliminary Remarks on Moral Regulation," Resources for Feminist Research 17, no. 3 (September 1988): 31–34.; Mariana Valverde, The Age of Light, Soap, and Water: Moral Reform in English Canada, 1885–1925 (Toronto: McClelland and Stewart, 1991; reissued Toronto: University of Toronto Press, 2008).; Mariana Valverde, ed., Studies in Moral Regulation (Toronto: Centre of Criminology, University of Toronto, 1994).; Carolyn Strange and Tina Loo, Making Good: Law and Moral Regulation in Canada, 1867–1939 (Toronto: University of Toronto Press, 1997).

strands.title: Sexual regulation and national security
strands.focus: Sexuality as an object of state regulation, from Kinsman's 1987 history to the Cold War security campaign against queers.
strands.works: Gary Kinsman, The Regulation of Desire: Sexuality in Canada (Montréal: Black Rose Books, 1987).; Gary Kinsman and Patrizia Gentile, The Canadian War on Queers: National Security as Sexual Regulation (Vancouver: UBC Press, 2010).

strands.title: Reproduction, eugenics and medicine
strands.focus: Contraception, abortion, eugenics and medical views of women's bodies.
strands.works: Angus McLaren and Arlene Tigar McLaren, The Bedroom and the State: The Changing Practices and Politics of Contraception and Abortion in Canada, 1880–1980 (Toronto, 1986).; Angus McLaren, Our Own Master Race: Eugenics in Canada, 1885–1945 (Toronto, 1990).; Wendy Mitchinson, The Nature of Their Bodies: Women and Their Doctors in Victorian Canada (Toronto: University of Toronto Press, 1991).

strands.title: Women, girls, welfare and the law
strands.focus: Legal, welfare and policing regimes directed at women and girls, in English Canada and Quebec.
strands.works: Andrée Lévesque, La norme et les déviantes: des femmes au Québec pendant l'entre-deux-guerres (Montréal: Éditions du Remue-ménage, 1989).; Constance Backhouse, Petticoats and Prejudice: Women and Law in Nineteenth-Century Canada (Toronto: Women's Press for the Osgoode Society, 1991).; Karen Dubinsky, Improper Advances: Rape and Heterosexual Conflict in Ontario, 1880–1929 (Chicago: University of Chicago Press, 1993).; Margaret Hillyard Little, "'Manhunts and Bingo Blabs': The Moral Regulation of Ontario Single Mothers," Canadian Journal of Sociology 19, no. 2 (1994): 233ff.; Carolyn Strange, Toronto's Girl Problem: The Perils and Pleasures of the City, 1880–1930 (Toronto: University of Toronto Press, 1995).; Joan Sangster, Regulating Girls and Women: Sexuality, Family, and the Law in Ontario, 1920–1960 (2001).

strands.title: Normality and the psy-sciences
strands.focus: Postwar psychology, schooling and youth as producers of heterosexual and familial norms.
strands.works: Mary Louise Adams, The Trouble with Normal: Postwar Youth and the Making of Heterosexuality (Toronto: University of Toronto Press, 1997).; Mona Gleason, Normalizing the Ideal: Psychology, Schooling, and the Family in Postwar Canada (Toronto: University of Toronto Press, 1999).

strands.title: Governmentality and reformulations
strands.focus: Critics and theorists recast moral regulation: Foucault's governmentality (Dean), self-formation and Lebensführung against a state-only model (Ruonavaara), Gramsci and all social relations (Hunt), freedom and the will (Valverde).
strands.works: Mitchell Dean, "'A Social Structure of Many Souls': Moral Regulation, Government, and Self-Formation," Canadian Journal of Sociology 19, no. 2 (1994): 145ff.; Alan Hunt, "Moral Regulation and Making-up the New Person," Theoretical Criminology 1, no. 3 (1997): 275–301.; Hannu Ruonavaara, "Moral Regulation: A Reformulation," Sociological Theory 15, no. 3 (1997): 277–293.; Mariana Valverde, Diseases of the Will: Alcohol and the Dilemmas of Freedom (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1998).; Alan Hunt, Governing Morals: A Social History of Moral Regulation (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1999).

proposed_relationships.relationship: Foucauldian analysis contributes to the concept of moral regulation and its governmentality reformulation
proposed_relationships.evidence_note: Ruonavaara's abstract describes Corrigan and Sayer's framework as fusing Durkheimian and Foucauldian analysis with basic Marxist theory; Dean's abstract argues that problems in Corrigan's account are better formulated through Foucault's problematic of governmentality. PhD context: 46 of 107 PhDs citing Valverde 1991 also cite Foucault (43% vs 20% of all PhDs). Drawn as a contribution, the atlas's usual kind for Foucault's outgoing edges; an influence edge would need Valverde's own acknowledgement of the debt, which was sought (2026-10-12) but not found in checked text. Not a claim about every Canadian study in the roster.

proposed_relationships.map_label: Corrigan and Sayer: The Great Arch
proposed_relationships.evidence_note: Ruonavaara: Corrigan and Sayer introduced moral regulation to sociological debate in their historical sociology of English state formation, The Great Arch (1985). Adams applies it to state formation through Ontario VD policy. Corrigan and Sayer are not in the historicalsociology roster; this edge records a contribution from comparative historical sociology, not membership.

proposed_relationships.relationship: Sexual regulation and the national-security campaign against queers
proposed_relationships.evidence_note: Kinsman's The Regulation of Desire (1987) and Kinsman and Gentile's history of the security campaign that spied on, interrogated and harassed gays and lesbians from the 1950s to the late 1990s (publisher page read) contribute Canadian studies of sexual regulation. Complements the queer entry's regulation strand; it does not claim Canadian priority.

proposed_relationships.relationship: Protestant reformers as regulators and as religious actors
proposed_relationships.evidence_note: Valverde studies the moral fervour of Protestant social reformers (publisher description); the religion-and-reform entry studies the same churches and social gospel as religious history (Christie and Gauvreau 1996, title-level). The two fields read the reformers differently; no critique is asserted because the checked texts do not state one. PhD context: 67 of 164 2009–2026 PhDs engaging moral_regulation also engage cdn_religion_reform (41%; lift 3.97), counted after removing shared anchors. Bibliographies record consultation, not influence; lifts are high for most Canadian pairs.

proposed_relationships.relationship: Women, girls, sexuality and the law
proposed_relationships.evidence_note: Feminist legal and sexual histories sit in both fields: Backhouse (1991), Lévesque (1989), Dubinsky (1993), Strange (1995), Sangster (2001), and Little's study of the moral scrutiny of single mothers (1994, abstract read). Shared people are rosters, not edges. PhD context: 136 of 155 2009–2026 PhDs engaging moral_regulation also engage cdn_women_gender (88%; lift 3.52), counted after removing shared anchors (Mitchinson). Bibliographies record consultation, not influence; lifts are high for most Canadian pairs.

Adams studies discourses on youth, delinquency, indecent literature and sex education as producers of heterosexual norms (publisher description); Gleason studies psychology and the normal family. PhD context: 74 of 142 2009–2026 PhDs engaging moral_regulation also engage cdn_childhood_youth (52%; lift 5.66), counted after removing shared anchors (Adams, Gleason). Bibliographies record consultation, not influence; lifts are high for most Canadian pairs.

proposed_relationships.relationship: Moral reform, racial purity and law
proposed_relationships.evidence_note: Valverde's reformers linked sexual health to racial purity (publisher description); Backhouse's Colour-Coded traces racism through law (title-level). PhD context: 72 of 149 2009–2026 PhDs engaging moral_regulation also engage cdn_immigration_ethnicity (48%; lift 3.99), counted after removing shared anchors (Backhouse). Bibliographies record consultation, not influence; lifts are high for most Canadian pairs.

proposed_relationships.relationship: Disease, eugenics and the body as objects of regulation
proposed_relationships.evidence_note: Adams reads Ontario's 1918 commission on venereal disease and feeble-mindedness as targeting bourgeois-defined immorality as much as infection (abstract). McLaren on eugenics and Mitchinson on women and their doctors are title-level. Comparison with the medical history entry, not a claim that medical history is regulatory history.

Already proposed by another drafter as lof_rel_08 (comparison) in drafts/liberal_order_framework; not duplicated. Evidence from this draft that could be merged into it: Boundary edge. The user decided (2026-10-12) that the liberal order framework is 'a different project closer to history of capitalism'. McKay's prospectus maps Canada as a project of liberal rule; moral regulation studies the governance of conduct and selves. They share state formation (Corrigan and Sayer; Adams; Curtis's census history), so a comparison rather than a contribution in either direction. PhD context: 40 of 112 2009–2026 PhDs engaging moral_regulation also engage liberal_order_framework (36%; lift 2.85), counted after removing shared anchors (Curtis, Valverde). Bibliographies record consultation, not influence; lifts are high for most Canadian pairs. Sources: cdnsrc_mckay_2000, cdnsrc_adams_1994, cdnsrc_curtis_2001.

open_questions: Label: 'Moral regulation & the regulatory state' (groups.json) or simply 'Moral regulation'? 'Regulatory state' could pull in the liberal order framework's state-formation work.
Valverde and Weir, 'The Struggles of the Immoral' (1988) is often treated as the first Canadian statement but could not be verified; it is kept out of the sources. Can the user check it?
Curtis is an anchor here but primary in liberal_order_framework. Keep him out of the roster (proposed) and mention him only in the boundary strand?
Foucault: proposed as an influence edge (foucault → moral_regulation), supported by Ruonavaara's and Dean's abstracts and the PhD co-citation. Is influence the right kind, or contribution?
Should Corrigan and Sayer also be added to the atlas's historicalsociology roster? They are not there now.
Backhouse is primary here (groups.json) but her most-cited book (Colour-Coded) anchors cdn_immigration_ethnicity. Confirm primary placement.

question_resolutions.summary: Label changed to 'Moral regulation'; 'regulatory state' would overlap the liberal order framework's state-formation work.

Valverde and Weir, 'The Struggles of the Immoral', Resources for Feminist Research 17, no. 3 (September 1988): 31–34 (reprinted in Glasbeek, ed., 2006, 75–84) is now a metadata-checked source (Weir's York publication record; Open Library for the Glasbeek spelling), added to the description, date label, Valverde's row, a new Lorna Weir row and the moral-reform strand. It is not called the first Canadian statement.
Curtis stays out of the roster and appears only in the state-formation boundary strand; his readers engage the liberal order framework (64%, lift 4.1) more than moral regulation (35%, lift 3.2).
mreg_rel_01 (foucault → moral_regulation) is now a contribution. A search for Valverde's own acknowledgement of Foucault found none in checked text, so it was not upgraded to influence.
Corrigan and Sayer are not proposed for the historicalsociology roster; that atlas entry is outside this packet. The contribution edge mreg_rel_02 records their role.

The data favour cdn_immigration_ethnicity as Backhouse's primary placement (Colour-Coded: 52 of her 81 citing PhDs; immigration readers 71%, lift 5.9), but the move is held for the user; her roster row and placement here are unchanged.
